concept.title: Pressure, speed and height trade along an ideal-flow path
concept.inferential_jump: Along a streamline in steady ideal flow, pressure, kinetic, and gravitational energy-per-volume contributions trade; a speed increase alone does not determine the pressure change unless the other contributions are controlled.
entry_assumptions: Can relate section area to flow speed for steady incompressible flow.
Can compare heights and distinguish static pressure from flow speed.

teaching_path.action: Choose two marked points on the same ideal-flow path and list three ledger columns at each point: static pressure, motion contribution, and height contribution.
teaching_path.why_valid: The comparison is only interpretable when both points belong to the same applicable flow path and all energy-per-volume contributions are kept visible.
teaching_path.output: point 1: pressure | motion | height ; point 2: pressure | motion | height

teaching_path.action: First narrow a horizontal section so speed rises while the two point heights remain equal.
teaching_path.why_valid: With height fixed in this controlled case, the increased motion contribution must be balanced by a decrease in the static-pressure contribution along the ideal-flow path.
teaching_path.output: horizontal narrowing: height = same; speed -> higher; static pressure -> lower

teaching_path.action: Now move the faster point to a lower height and ask whether speed alone still fixes the pressure ordering.
teaching_path.why_valid: Changing height adds another ledger change, so the earlier two-variable conclusion cannot be transferred without considering the full comparison.
teaching_path.output: speed at point 2: higher | height at point 2: lower | pressure ordering: not decidable from speed alone

predict.prompt: Point 2 on an ideal-flow path has higher speed than point 1, but it is also lower. Can you conclude immediately that its static pressure is lower?
predict.defensible_answer: No. Height changed too, so the full energy-per-volume ledger must be considered before ranking the pressures.

attempt.produces: A two-point three-column ledger marking which of pressure, motion, and height contributions are known to rise, fall, or remain unknown.

rubric.criterion: The speed change is recorded in the motion column rather than turned directly into a pressure verdict.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner keeps separate contributions separate.

rubric.criterion: The height change is recorded before pressure is ranked.
rubric.evidence_of: The learner recognizes why the horizontal special case cannot be overgeneralized.

accepted: The ledger marks motion higher and height lower at point 2, leaving static pressure to be determined from the complete balance rather than from speed alone.
rejected: The response writes 'faster means lower pressure' immediately and ignores the changed height.

route.ask: Which three contributions must be kept visible at each comparison point?
route.why_this_ask: It prevents the learner from reducing the situation to a pressure-speed slogan.

route.ask: What does a horizontal narrowing show when height is deliberately held fixed?
route.why_this_ask: It establishes the familiar special case under controlled conditions.

route.ask: What extra contribution changes when the faster point is also lower?
route.why_this_ask: It creates the reason the special-case inference can fail.

route.ask: Can speed alone still decide the pressure ordering?
route.why_this_ask: The learner must withdraw the overgeneralization explicitly.

reconstruct.differs_from_teaching_path: The declarative path builds a full ledger, demonstrates the horizontal special case, then breaks one held condition; the elicitation starts from the tempting pressure slogan and makes the learner discover which missing column blocks it.

boundary_test.prompt: If the fluid has substantial dissipative loss between the two points, is this ideal-flow ledger sufficient by itself?
boundary_test.answer: No. The rung's comparison assumes the stated ideal-flow model; appreciable loss means the model choice must be reconsidered.
boundary_test.confirms: The learner treats the pressure-speed relation as conditional on both the full ledger and the model assumptions.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Wherever fluid speed is higher, static pressure must be lower, regardless of height or losses.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Point 2 has higher speed than point 1 but is also much lower. Can speed alone determine which point has higher pressure?
misconceptions.repair: Use all Bernoulli terms between points on the same streamline and state the ideal-flow assumptions before drawing a pressure conclusion.

exit_task.prompt: Two points lie on one steady ideal-flow path. Point 2 has higher speed and lower height than point 1. Explain why speed alone is insufficient to rank the static pressures and identify what must be considered.

answer.summary: The static-pressure ordering cannot be inferred from speed alone because both the motion contribution and the height contribution change between the points; the complete ideal-flow energy ledger must be compared.
reasoning: A higher speed increases the motion contribution at point 2.
A lower height decreases the gravitational contribution at point 2.
Those two changes act in different parts of the ledger, so static pressure must be determined from the whole balance rather than a slogan about speed.
answer.check: Return the two points to equal height while keeping the ideal-flow assumptions; only then does the controlled horizontal narrowing support the simpler higher-speed/lower-static-pressure comparison.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: The exit answer identifies which qualitative energy contributions change and does not calculate a pressure value.
